slides.title: Three ideas carry most of ML
points: Probability describes uncertainty; linear algebra describes data as vectors and matrices; gradients describe how to improve a model step by step.
You need working intuition for each, not a maths degree.

slides.title: Vectors, distributions, slopes
points: A data point is a vector of numbers; a dataset is a matrix; a layer of a neural network multiplies by a matrix.
A dot product measures how aligned two vectors are; it's behind similarity search and attention.
Probability distributions describe likely values; a model's output is often a probability.
A gradient points in the direction that increases the error fastest; gradient descent steps the other way to reduce it.

slides.title: Intuition before formulas
points: Skipping the maths leaves you unable to debug a model that won't train.
Going deep before building anything stalls progress; learn the idea, then use it.
Libraries compute gradients for you (automatic differentiation), but you still choose the learning rate.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Loss curves: if the loss explodes, the learning rate is usually too high; if it barely moves, too low.
Embeddings compared by cosine similarity.
Numbers kept on similar scales (normalisation) so training is stable.

points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Measuring on data the model hasn't seen
points: A model is trained on one part of the data, tuned on a second, and judged once on a third.
Only the untouched test set tells you how it will do on new data.

slides.title: Three sets, three jobs
points: Training set: the model learns from it.
Validation set: you compare models and choose settings (hyperparameters) with it.
Test set: used once at the end, for an honest estimate.
Cross-validation rotates the validation set through the data when data is scarce.

slides.title: Splitting the right way
points: Random splits leak when rows are related: the same user in train and test, or future data in train.
Split by time for anything that predicts the future, and by group for repeated entities.
Looking at the test set repeatedly turns it into a validation set.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: A fixed, versioned test set so results compare across months.
Splits done before any feature engineering that uses statistics of the data.
Results reported on the test set once, with the validation history kept.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Two ways models fool you
points: Overfitting: the model memorises training data, noise included, and does worse on new data.
Leakage: information that won't exist at prediction time sneaks into training, making results look too good.

slides.title: Spot and prevent
points: Overfitting shows as training error far below validation error.
Fixes: more data, a simpler model, regularisation (penalising large weights), dropout, early stopping.
Leakage comes from features computed after the outcome, duplicates across splits, or preprocessing fitted on all data.
Ask of each feature: would I know this at the moment I predict?

slides.title: Too simple or too clever
points: A model that's too simple underfits: poor on training and validation alike.
Aggressive regularisation trades some accuracy for reliability.
Suspiciously good results deserve suspicion first.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Learning curves plotted for training and validation together.
Preprocessing fitted only on training data, inside a pipeline.
A review of features against the prediction timeline.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Choosing what 'good' means
points: A metric turns predictions into a score; the right one reflects the cost of the mistakes in the real decision.
Training uses a loss function; evaluation uses metrics people understand.

slides.title: Match the metric to the task
points: Classification: precision, recall, F1, ROC AUC, PR AUC (better when positives are rare).
Regression: MAE, RMSE, and error by segment.
Ranking: precision at k, NDCG.
Calibration: do predicted probabilities match observed frequencies?

slides.title: One number hides a lot
points: Averages across groups can hide a model that fails one group.
Offline gains don't always become online gains.
Optimising a proxy metric too hard drifts from the real goal.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: A primary metric plus guardrails, agreed before modelling.
Slices: performance by region, device, new versus returning users.
Offline evaluation followed by an online A/B test.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Inputs computed the same way, every time
points: A feature pipeline turns raw data into the model's inputs, for training and for live predictions.
If the two paths compute a feature differently, the model sees something new in production.

slides.title: One definition, two uses
points: Training-serving skew: a feature computed one way in a batch job and another in the live service.
Point-in-time correctness: training features must use only data available at that past moment.
A feature store keeps feature definitions, an offline store for training and an online store for fast lookups.
Features are versioned so models know exactly what they were trained on.

slides.title: Infrastructure against speed
points: A feature store is a lot of machinery for one model; it pays off when many models share features.
Real-time features are powerful and expensive to keep fresh.
Simple shared code for both paths can be enough at first.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: The same function used in training and serving.
Monitoring of feature values in production against training.
Backfills of a new feature with point-in-time joins.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: When one machine isn't enough
points: Large models and datasets need several GPUs or machines, for memory and for time.
The work is splitting data and model sensibly and keeping the hardware busy.

slides.title: Data and model parallelism
points: Data parallelism: each GPU holds the whole model and trains on a different slice of the batch; gradients are averaged.
Model parallelism: the model itself is split across GPUs when it doesn't fit on one.
Mixed precision (16-bit numbers) cuts memory and time with little loss of accuracy.
Checkpoints save progress, so a failure doesn't lose days.

slides.title: Speed against cost and complexity
points: Communication between GPUs can become the bottleneck.
Bigger batches change training dynamics; learning rates need adjusting.
Cloud GPUs are expensive; a smaller model trained well often beats a bigger one trained badly.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: PyTorch DDP or FSDP, or a managed training service.
Experiments tracked (MLflow, Weights & Biases) with code, data and settings.
GPU use monitored: idle GPUs usually mean slow data loading.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Predictions in production
points: Serving puts a trained model behind an API or into a batch job, so products can use its predictions.
It's ordinary software engineering with extra concerns: latency, cost and versions.

slides.title: Online, batch, versions
points: Online serving answers one request in milliseconds; batch scoring precomputes predictions for everyone on a schedule.
Batching requests together uses the hardware better, at a small latency cost.
Models are versioned and deployed like code, with canaries or shadow traffic before full rollout.
Smaller or quantised models cut latency and cost.

slides.title: Fresh, fast, cheap: pick carefully
points: Batch predictions are cheap and can be stale; online ones are fresh and costly.
Bigger models are often more accurate and slower; measure whether the gain is worth it.
A fallback is needed when the model service is down.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Shadow deployments: the new model runs alongside the old, its answers logged but not used.
p95 and p99 latency budgets per endpoint.
Inputs and outputs logged (without personal data) for monitoring and retraining.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Models decay quietly
points: The world changes after a model is trained; its inputs and the relationships it learned drift.
Monitoring catches the decline before users or the business feel it.

slides.title: What to watch
points: Data drift: input distributions change (new devices, new markets).
Concept drift: the relationship between inputs and outcome changes (fraud tactics evolve).
Watch inputs, prediction distributions, and real outcomes when labels arrive.
Retrain on a schedule or when drift crosses a threshold, then evaluate before deploying.

slides.title: Alerts that matter
points: Labels often arrive late (did the loan default?), so quality is seen only after a delay.
Drift alerts on every feature are noisy; focus on important features and outcomes.
Automatic retraining can learn from bad data; keep a check before deploying.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Dashboards of key feature distributions against training.
A delayed-label quality report each week.
A rollback path to the previous model version.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

newQuestions.stem: During training, the loss jumps around wildly and then becomes NaN. What's the most likely first fix?
choices: Lower the learning rate (and check for unscaled inputs)
Use a bigger batch of the same data
why: Steps that are too large overshoot and diverge.
More capacity doesn't fix divergence.
It'll keep diverging.
It can help a little, but the step size is the usual cause.

newQuestions.stem: A model predicting next month's sales was evaluated with a random split of 3 years of data, and scored far better than it does in production. Why?
choices: Random splitting put future months in training, so the model saw information it won't have; split by time
The test set was too large
why: Training on the future leaks; a time split mirrors real use.
Not inevitably; the split caused it.
Size isn't the issue.
Size of the test set doesn't inflate scores.

newQuestions.stem: Scaling (mean and standard deviation) was computed on the whole dataset before splitting. What's the problem?
choices: Leakage: statistics from the test set shaped training; fit the scaler on training data only
The data will be too small
why: Test information slipped into training, flattering results.
It's a classic leak.
It doesn't cause underfitting.
Size doesn't change.

newQuestions.stem: A model screening for a rare disease must miss as few cases as possible; follow-up tests are cheap. Which metric matters most?
why: Missing a case is the costly mistake; recall measures how many cases are caught.
Accuracy is dominated by the many healthy cases.
False alarms are cheap here.
Not an evaluation metric.

newQuestions.stem: A model works well offline but poorly live. You find 'average order value' is computed over 90 days in training and 30 days in the live service. What is this?
choices: Training-serving skew; compute the feature from one shared definition
why: The model is fed a different feature than it learned.
It isn't about the model's fit.
A seed wouldn't cause this.
It's a bug.

newQuestions.stem: Training on 8 GPUs shows each GPU busy only 30 % of the time. What's the usual cause to check first?
choices: The input pipeline: data loading and preprocessing can't keep up; add workers, cache, or preprocess ahead
why: GPUs wait for data when loading is the bottleneck.
It may be wasteful, but loading is the usual culprit.
Not related.
It affects learning, not utilisation.

newQuestions.stem: You want to check a new model on real traffic without risking users. What's the safest approach?
choices: Shadow deployment: run it alongside the current model, log its predictions, and compare before switching
Test it only on last year's data
why: Real inputs, no effect on users, and a direct comparison.
Risky with no comparison.
Offline tests miss today's traffic.
Self-selected users aren't representative.

newQuestions.stem: A fraud model's precision has fallen steadily over three months, with no code changes. What's the likely cause and response?
choices: Concept drift as fraud patterns changed; investigate recent cases, retrain on fresh labelled data, and evaluate before deploying
A bug introduced three months ago
The model ran out of memory
why: Adversaries adapt; models trained on old patterns decay.
Nothing changed in the code.
More data doesn't cause gradual decline.
That would cause errors, not a slow drift.
